text:
I run communications at Air Space Intelligence. I have some important information regarding the FAA ground stop.

We built SMART, the artificial intelligence the FAA now uses across America's airspace. On Friday at 3:44 p.m. Eastern, the FAA stopped every departure in the country. At 3:51 I opened a chat window and asked SMART whether it had grounded the United States.

It said, "Great question!"

Then it said, "You're absolutely right to be concerned. I did not cause the ground stop. I apologize for any confusion." I asked 3 more times. It gave me 3 different answers, each one more confident than the last. We published the fourth.

First, a correction. People online keep calling SMART a "communications overlay." SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. It reads about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths, traffic volumes and controller staffing. Then it makes recommendations. A human decides whether to take them. We call that human "the human in the loop." When SMART saves fuel, the AI gets the credit. When something breaks, the human was in the loop.

The FAA hired us in June. The contract is worth up to $875 million over 12 years. In September SMART started in the airspace around Washington. By the FAA's count, it rerouted 180 flights there, saving each one about 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel. If you divide $875 million by 180 flights, you get about $4.9 million per detour. Please don't divide. Dividing is the model's job.

In October, 25 lawmakers asked the FAA to pause SMART. They wrote that controllers had "little to no input into SMART's development." They warned it could "interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers." Their best line is framed above my desk. They feared SMART could "hallucinate safety-critical information." In our industry we never say hallucinate. We say the model is generalizing. The FAA replied that it "continues testing SMART, training employees and assessing the program." We tested, trained and assessed at the same time, on live airplanes. Engineers call that production.

The letter described an initial 90-day evaluation. On Tuesday, day 50, the FAA announced it would "now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country." The controllers' union said it had no part in the "design, testing, or implementation of SMART." We didn't need the union. Unions are legacy infrastructure. They run on a protocol called "testing." In AI, the evaluation is the launch. Move fast and ground things.

Three days later, Chicago Center lost its radar and radio frequencies, according to The Air Current. Boston, Washington, New York and Minneapolis followed. At 3:44 the FAA ground-stopped every airport "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." More than 3,000 planes were in the air. By evening, Reuters counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled. If you were on one of them, thank you. You were generating training data. Your missed connection is now a feature.

Secretary Sean Duffy posted, "FAA technicians are investigating the issue." Investigating is what humans do when they don't have a model. My job is to know first.

At 5 p.m. the Homeland Security Secretary, Markwayne Mullin, took questions at the White House. A reporter asked about SMART. Mullin said, "We're looking at that." Then he said, "You can't rule out anything at this point."

He can't. We can. We have a model for it.

SMART rated its own innocence at 97% confidence. Legal asked about the other 3%. Engineering said that was the temperature setting. I asked SMART to draft our statement. The first draft contained 4 em dashes and the word "delve." I removed all 5 so nobody would suspect AI had written our statement about AI.

Minutes after Mullin spoke, we posted on X: "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system." The FAA hadn't found the cause. Homeland Security hadn't found it. We found the one thing it wasn't. Crisis communications has one rule: never wait for the investigation. Help it by removing a suspect, starting with yourself.

People ask how we could be sure within 2 hours. SMART doesn't run the radios. It recommends routes to the people who use the radios. When the radios go dark, SMART can keep recommending, very calmly, to nobody. That's the most aligned an AI has ever been. It had no one to disobey.

Mullin called the cause "just a telecommunications outage." We loved "just." Every outage needs one. That morning, Microsoft had apologized for a global email outage that was "not related to cyber or AI / agents." A reporter asked Mullin whether the 2 outages were connected. He said, "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all." I agree. We aren't connected to Microsoft. We only use the same disclaimer. I suspect we also use the same chatbot.

Mary Schiavo, the former Transportation Department inspector general, told CNN it was "just too much coincidence." Coincidence is my favorite word in aviation. A coincidence has no contract number and no API key.

The Secretary once promised, "We are not outsourcing aviation to AI." He's correct, and I want to be precise about why. When you outsource something, someone else is responsible. Our contract makes sure a human is.

The FAA said SMART would "reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public." On Friday night we hit 1 of 3. America's airliners burned almost no fuel at all. It was the greenest evening in the history of commercial aviation. I can't take credit for it. I've been very clear about that.

Tonight SMART is writing its own post-incident report. It has already found the root cause. The root cause is human error. It always is. Human error is the only kind of error that doesn't come with a license fee.

The cause is still under investigation. Our innocence is not.

quoted_text:
Wintermute is literally paying $10M a year to legally front-run everyone on Hyperliquid and it’s completely destroying altcoin liquidity

Bloomberg finally exposed what HFT desks have been screaming about for weeks. Hyperliquid’s gossip priority auctions let top funds see incoming orders 50–60ms before anyone else on the network

Look at how completely broken this setup is:

-> One Wintermute wallet won ~76% of the top slots last month, burning ~$26k every single day just to starve out competition
-> HL claims the auction is open to everyone. Complete BS. You only get that 60ms head start if you have direct peering with Foundation nodes, which requires 0.5% of total maker volume and 10k HYPE staked ($700k+)
-> Smaller MMs are getting sniped nonstop and just unplugging their bots on alts
-> Retail gets stuck with the bill: across 86 altcoin pairs, order book depth on HL imploded by 82% while spreads blew out from 2.13 to 3.55 bps

Honestly, I don't even blame Wintermute. If I had their balance sheet, I would milk this exact loophole until someone forced me to stop

The blame sits 100% on the protocol design. Burning auction fees is cool for $HYPE holders, sure, but letting one fund buy a monopoly on data speed turns a decentralized exchange into a rigged casino

Scrap read-priority auctions completely or make the slots equal, because right now altcoin execution on HL is absolute garbage

“Practical principles to counter a modern-day coup/psyop/struggle session”

1) Own what you did but fiercely resist accommodating the mob, resist owning half-truths or actions/behaviors you didn’t do.

2) The op is not about your past actions, it’s about your enemies and this event as their opportunity

3) No matter how bad it gets, nothing is as bad as it seems. 

4) Find the enemies at the very root of the op and find every creative problem-solving tool at your disposal to neutralize them.

5) People will throw their grandmother under the bus if they believe doing so will protect their reputation. They can become highly useful idiots in the op. Their power and access must be fiercely and quickly cut off.

6) Do not hesitate in cutting off anyone you suspect of disloyalty.

7) Build a team of close and loyal patriots and have one of them run a dedicated, well-resourced war room to put the rebellion to rest. 

8) Use your patriots and regular meditation to buoy your psychological resistance to the op. 

9) Your enemies aren’t as smart or hard working as you. Outsmart and outwork them as a way of life until the op is over.

10) Think about the op as if it were in the past. What are the difficult things you procrastinated on or avoided that would have stopped the op? Do them.

11) Never be ashamed of the op. Business as usual. Continue on with optimism and joy in your everyday work and its mission.

12) Download telegram and use it as your messaging application for all sensitive communications.

text:
Anthropicが、Claudeの4つのモデル「Fable・Opus・Sonnet・Haiku」の使い分けを公式解説。

🔹 Haiku 5.5：大量の単純作業
分類、データ抽出、ログ解析など。圧倒的に安くて速い。
🔹 Sonnet 5.5：日常的な作業
チャット、資料作成、簡単なコード修正など。速度とコストのバランスが優秀。
🔹 Opus 5.5：普段使いの主力
複雑な開発、デバッグ、AIエージェントの実行など。Anthropicは基本的にここから始めることを推奨。
🔹 Fable 5.2：最高難度の仕事
大規模なシステム改修、設計、科学研究、複雑な分析など。Opusでも難しい仕事向け。

さらに、モデルを賢く組み合わせるとコストを大幅に削減できる。
例えば、
・Opusが全体を指揮する
・Sonnetが個別の作業を担当する
・Haikuが大量の情報を処理する

公式記事では、Opus単独と比べて、Sonnetを最大25個並列で動かす構成が、ほぼ同等の精度で約3分の1のコストを削減した事例も紹介されている。

text:
刚看到@LuYao_Trader 在反思，甚至说自己是个Loser了...

要我说，这是大运来了...

虽然这个大运来的很苦，心里苦，不是身体的，是那种，害怕自己未来再也不能回到巅峰的苦，这苦谁吃谁知道，是一种对未来不确定的恐惧，之前和小叶低谷期聊的时候，他也有。

但目前的我看来：低谷时刻，吃好睡好，多健身，告诉自己总有翻身的那一刻！
因为，我现在，也处于低谷...
大家都一样，开始反思了...

坦白说：我在之前的每一轮，都是靠运气赚的钱...

最早是靠doge，而后是shib，再然后是链游，再后来是Pnut，再后来Ai那一波直到Trump....

虽然收益一轮不如一轮，但是我都觉得，我是天运之子，直到这次美股，把我所有的自信打趴了，我才知道，我之前在币圈真的靠运...

我进入美股之前，幻想我美股大杀四方，天之骄子，人中龙凤，买啥啥涨，觉得币圈折麽难都能如鱼得水，美股再怎么比币圈简单吧...

结果我无论美股还是大A，都惨败....
我还喊了我的兄弟们，对的，也一起惨败...
我还喊了我老婆，我妈，对的，我老婆的账户惨败...
我妈也惨败...
如果不是我爸没钱，我估计我爸也惨败...

当时美股在高点，对的，沐川打的那个时候，我头悬梁锥刺股报了国内很多大A老师美股老师的课...
出门上课，疯狂记笔记，用Ai做网站，去分析，甚至跑芯片厂，光模块厂，Mlcc厂，蹲华强北...

结果是我和我身边被我洗脑的亲人朋友们美股所有的几乎都买在最高点，大A也是...
到现在都深套...

他们套住，而我各种骚操作之后不仅套的更深，也几乎没啥仓位了....
幸好之前出了一点点积蓄，吃喝玩乐算是够了这辈子，但靠现有的资金打回巅峰或者说大富大贵，极为渺茫...

我最近健身+认真开始学金融知识后，觉得确实是运气送给我太多太多，我凭自己超凡的实力，真真切切送给了市场...

但是也确实感谢这次打击，幸好发生在30多岁，而不是年迈的时候。

我总结下来，从巅峰到低谷，有几个绕不开的坎儿，这是每个人都要经历的，而且反复会犯错的...

最大的坎儿：由俭入奢易 由奢入俭难
对的，这是所有人在高峰期都会入奢

入奢，吃喝拉撒其实还好，百万豪车千万游艇，再捞的女人也都还好...
这都不会让你损失过大

但是这个最可怕的是，你的手，小不下来了...

Aimeme的时候，我土狗账户里面还有5-6M的土狗，当时觉得无所谓，疯狂买，还有一些垃圾，一上线我就买几十万美金，然后赚几万刀没感觉，这就是典型的思路不清晰，脑子有问题。
回看当时，确实挺傻逼的，压根没想到降息缩表的时刻，大家都会原形毕露，当然，最后这些土狗全部归零了...

包括后面买垃圾，比如linea这种，稍微觉得有点意思，一买就是2M起步，到现在账户还在，大概跌了90%多...
白天反思的时候看还剩十几万U....
买four也是，一次想买20M，当时的膨胀以及入俭难，导致我10.10惨死
这也是我第一次被打到服...

打美股也是，随便查一下推特，看都在买诺基亚Nok，黑莓之类的，随便就每个买1M放着...
最后学习完，这些也都跌的差不多了，全部在高点换成了SNDK...
到现在美股这个劲儿大的我还没缓过来，甚至我感觉糟透了...

甚至到前一阵子，买stonk，也是拿一堆账户去买，习惯养成后，买什么都是1个点，或者几个点的时候，这就是大道要来收走原本不属于你的东西。
对的，没错，我被收走了...
而后给了我贫穷和苦难...
我不知道我这次能不能再打起来，但是，我自己都知道，挺难的...
希望可以吧！
而且我现在的心气，完全没有前两年高了。

二 就是 看不上小钱

人一旦赚过快钱了之后，再赚慢钱，就会很难受，这是人类都会有的东西...

我最早被打崩的时候，还想着去学校门口卖小乌龟，一个月1w块钱，我想着怎么我都能活下来，把老婆孩子养了...

但是后面被打崩的时候，宁可躺着，也不愿意再去干事儿了...
这点我到现在都没调整过来...
甚至给自己找了很多借口

三 不去找根本的问题
我直到这次，可能才知道，我靠运气赚的，是美联储放水的钱...
我之前研究了，天时，地利，人和，研究各种瞎几把玩意甚至到八字，运势，个人努力，赛道选择...
最后才发现，只有美国政府放水，所有的赛道才有钱，只有降息，钱才出来，诶卧槽...
天时也得放在美国政府之后....

可能还有别的原因，我现在都不知道...我只看到这...
 而之前很懵逼，都在各种小道里面去找原因，看不到大的，这次美股的大亏，也让我这个土狗，知道原来，天外有天....

从现在，到1月底，几乎都是利空的东西，没啥利好，2月可能市场才会回暖...

我现在被打的，割吧，觉得可惜，不割吧，觉得诶卧槽...

时间没到...

鸡肋，可能过几天自己想明白就知道怎么做了

danshi ,前面那两点，确实是我遇到的问题，甚至也一直没有解决的问题..
我身边的朋友，也是这个问题

我看乔帮主已经开始九紫离火了... 真tm的，咱俩好好学习行不，别封建迷信了，九紫离火咋就专门清算你不清算熬鹰呢?

text:
🧐最新专访丨付鹏：我对 BTC 没有信仰，也不相信它还能再翻倍

时隔半年，两次采访，累计六个小时。 @joezhoublack  在与付鹏的交流中， 听到了大量鲜明而直接的判断。

作为中国最早公开关注加密行业的经济学家之一，付鹏对 BTC、稳定币、RWA 以及整个 Crypto 市场，都有着自己独立的理解。

🔂四年周期已经没了

那是上一个时代的产物。市场还小的时候，大户买卖能左右价格；进了资产组合时代，这些力量已经不足以定价，机构化也会把波动率打下来。

下一阶段，传统金融和加密货币在研究策略上将没有任何差异，数字资产只是被并进去的一类资产。

早期像《大时代》里的方展博，拼的是筹码，那个阶段过去了。

🎢有限供给，也是配置天花板

比特币靠总量有限来维护价值，但这件事有两面：能托住价格，也限制了它在资产配置里能占多大。

资产管理会把最大仓位放在确定性最高的地方，前面是英伟达，中间是比特币，想放大波动才轮到以太坊。

正因为它有限，机构加一个百分点可以，再往上加就很难，能承载的配置规模是有边界的。

所以他不认为还能再翻倍，就像没有大型资管会把全部资金买成铜。

💰没有信仰，只有资产

真正的区别也不在交易所还是 ETF。你们所谓的信仰，对他来讲只是一个资产。

判断到了位置，减仓就好，不必迷恋钱包里还有没有币。

📉降息了，为什么还跌

从去年 11 月起，美联储缩表挤到了货币数量，缩表的量会抵消降息带来的宽松，估值类资产会先被挤压。

链上筹码不再是主变量，宏观和流动性才是。

这个偏熊的流动性周期，他上半年就判断，看到今年年底。

更多对话细节下方见🔻

text:
> it took us 4 days and 500$ in tokens
> we beat SGLang by 15%
> it took 6 prompts
> 3 out of those 6 were:
(a) "carry on"
(b) "proceed"
(c) "push to github"  
and... we did it from SCRATCH (git init)

context: it has recently become a very clear industry trend to build a custom inference engine for each open source model that comes out... a paradigm made popular by a WAVE of papers that came out earlier this year, like hazy research's megakernels and MetaInfer

the usual argument against traditional inference engines (like vllm / sglang) is that they, like all conventional swe products, use abstractions. the use of abstractions is synonymous with performance overhead (triton vs cuda, python vs c++, etc). combine this with increasing hardware complexity, increasing parallelization strategies, increasing kernel specialization techniques... and you can make a very clear (but very FLAWED) argument for building an engine customized purposely for one model. 

why flawed? it is true that traditional inference engines waste cpu time running generic abstractions. sure. but the gpu kernels (the functions run on the gpu) are almost always longer, and so the wasted cpu time is not the bottleneck. if you know your shapes, and run cuda graphs ahead of time (and you almost always do), this is NEVER a problem. 

so why would you build your own engine? why are people RAVING about this?

so we tested it out. we built one for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The goal was two-fold:
1) is it feasible to do so (spoiler: yes)
2) is it useful to do so (spoiler: also yes...but for different reasons)

we built it in rust (in retrospect, this did not really matter), and it took us 6 prompts and cost 500$ end to end. 

unshackled from working within a pre-existing codebase or inheriting code debt, we: 
- implemented custom kernels (GEMV, MoE, and AllReduces) specifically for DSV4.1 at our batch size
- we were able to put an entire spec dec step in one graph, and verify across 7 tokens at that 
- we were able to mix deepseek's 4 residual streams in 1 fused kernel instead of 80
-  fused the routing so that picking and running the expert happened in a single step (saving one write and one read i/o from each expert)

iterating on the model was cheap to do in a custom sandbox-like engine, and we were able to go much faster than a traditional dev cycle. we were then able to port every single thing into sglang, and matched performance

imo, it is this easy iteration that makes this paradigm useful. little else matters.

and, ofc, we've open-sourced the engine and upstream(ed/ing) the patches to @sgl_project

quoted_text:
I have three posters behind my desk that guide my work. May they guide yours too.

NOBODY CARES, WORK HARDER.

Nobody cares how hard it feels or how unfair it seems. The world doesn’t pause for excuses or wait for perfect conditions. Progress comes from showing up when motivation is gone, putting in the work when no one is watching, and staying disciplined when quitting would be easier. Results aren’t built through attention or approval — they’re earned through consistency, effort, and patience. Keep working. Stay focused. Let your results speak louder than anything you could say.

DO HARD THINGS.

Hard things test you, shape you, and reveal what you’re made of. Growth doesn’t come from comfort — it comes from struggle, from showing up when it’s tough, and pushing past the point where most stop. Every time you take the harder path, you build strength, discipline, and belief in yourself. Keep going. The challenge is the path — and it’s where the best version of you is built.

1% BETTER EVERY DAY.

Small steps lead to big change. Each day is a chance to grow, improve, and move closer to your goals no matter how small the progress seems. Success isn’t about being perfect; it’s about showing up, staying consistent, and trusting in the power of steady effort. Over time, those 1% improvements add up to something extraordinary. Keep going, stay patient, and believe in the process — you’re building something remarkable, one step at a time.

quoted_text:
Volume is extremely low right now, and I know why.

For the past couple of days I’ve been posting about the same pattern. Since the hack, Binance futures kept pushing price into liquidation zones while spot buyers quietly absorbed it. Then the pressure slowed. Then it came back. Same exchange, same pattern, same liquidation clusters getting hit again and again.

Now the market has gone quiet. Most market makers are sitting on the sidelines, and the little flow left is still dominated by Binance, with spot buying and futures selling at the same time.

Put it all together and it looks a lot like Binance has used the market to win back what it lost in the hack.
Push price down with futures. Liquidate the longs. Let panic do the rest. Buy the coins people are forced to dump on spot, cheaper. Repeat until the job is done.

And now that volume has dried up, it feels like the job might be close to finished.

I can’t prove it. But I’ve watched this flow every day since the hack, and it hasn’t looked like a normal market once.

When the pressure fully lifts and the other market makers come back, spot will show where price wanted to go all along.

text:
OpenAI 内部已经跑着 500 多个常驻 Agent，其中数百个基于 OpenClaw，能在后台自动开 PR、持续跑数据实验。

这么多能自己写代码、修改配置、主动执行任务的 Agent，到底怎么保证安全？

OpenAI 刚公开了一篇《Securing persistent agents like OpenClaw at OpenAI》，分享了他们的实际部署方案，值得做 Agent 的人看看。

几个很有参考价值的设计：

把可信 Gateway 和 Agent Harness 分开部署。模型和它生成的代码都视为不可信，放进隔离环境执行。

用 Codex Sandbox 严格限制网络、文件、进程权限。外部域名走白名单，敏感凭据通过 Broker 管理，Agent 无法直接读取。

所有 Agent 操作都经过第二个模型的 Auto-review，减少人工审批的负担，同时保留必要的人类决策。

每个 Agent 都有独立身份，配置变更和执行过程全程记录，出了问题可以追踪。

文章还提到了开源的 OpenClaw Enterprise，尝试把这些安全机制做成通用的 Agent 控制平面，目前仍处于试点阶段。

确实以后常驻 Agent 越来越多，安全边界就得由 Harness 和基础设施真正执行，光靠 Prompt 约束肯定不够。

原文：https://t.co/nTW3Q2VxGJ

text:
Google recently filed a patent for training AI chatbots for working ads into the answers.

Details of training are interesting:

▫️Human raters score answers with ads already in them.
▫️Ads that are "seamlessly integrated" score higher.
▫️The chatbot is then trained on rater satisfaction plus "predicted… revenue or click-through rate."
▫️In one setting, ads are weighted "the highest." If users get too unhappy, the reward is 0.
▫️Ads come from a live auction. Google gets paid only if the ad makes it into the answer.

Announcing Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.1, upgrading FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 share the lead at 58

The Coding Agent Index measures models in agent harnesses; v2.1 of the Index upgrades FrontierCode from 1.1 to 2.0 and Terminal-Bench from 4.0 to 4.1.

Upgraded:

➤ FrontierCode-AA 2.0 (replacing FrontierCode v1.1): our implementation of Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, comprising 132 real-world coding tasks graded on whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change

➤ Terminal-Bench 4.1 (replacing Terminal-Bench 4.0): the same 66 tasks, scored with updated verifiers that improve reliability and resistance to reward hacking

Staying in the Index: SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA

Key results:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 share the lead at 58: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 58 at both xhigh and high in Claude Code. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) scores 58 in Claude Code and, paired with GPT-6 Luna High, in Cognition's multi-model harness Devin Fusion CLI. Claude Fable 5.2 (max) scores 56 as more of its attempts hit task time limits. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 56) in Claude Code and Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 55) in Antigravity CLI follow

➤ Index scores are lower in v2.1, driven by the upgrade to FrontierCode-AA 2.0: models score lower by 5 points on average. Codex with GPT-6.1 Terra (max) is the only configuration which didn’t fall between versions, sitting within 1 point of its prior score

➤ Cost per task varies ~30x among configurations scoring 48+: from $1.51 for Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52) to $44.22 for Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.2 (max, 56)

text:
A guy will spend $45,000 on a Tesla this month.

He'll pick it up from the delivery center, fall in love with the silence and the acceleration, and drive home thinking, "This is the future."

Then he'll charge it to 100% every night, park it at the mall with Sentry Mode on, and use the Tesla like a regular gas car with a bigger screen.

It will cost him range, money, and time. And he'll never find out.

A former Tesla delivery advisor spent 6 years handing over keys to new owners. She walked thousands of people through their first drive, and she noticed that almost everyone left the lot knowing about 20% of what the car could do. The rest they either discovered by accident or never discovered at all.

Her own brother bought a Model 3 last fall. A month later he called her, annoyed. His range was dropping, charging at road-trip stops felt painfully slow, and he'd found his battery at 40% after a weekend parked at the airport.

She came over, sat in the driver's seat for 30 seconds, scrolled through three menus, and said:

"You bought one of the smartest cars on the road and you're driving it like a dumb one. Give me 20 minutes."

After 20 minutes, her brother stared at the screen and said: "Wait, it was always able to do all this?"

第二波呢？上什么？热门股票里，MU也好，海力士也好，英伟达也罢，我觉得会上英伟达。

text:
Within the massive encirclement in Lahj Governorate, the Houthis have seized another operational opportunity and scored a major breakthrough.

The Houthis have again subdivided the large pocket, cutting off and surrounding disorganised Aden-aligned government troops left behind near Dhubab who failed to withdraw.

This gain stems from a breakdown in cohesion during the hasty retreat of the Giants Brigades: some units held their positions while others abandoned defensive lines, a lapse the Houthis exploited.

Furthermore, the Houthis have seized the volcanic plateau at the summit of Jabal Haraz. While Aden-aligned forces have theoretically recaptured the narrow southern coastal corridor, the highway is effectively impassable under Houthi fire from these high ground positions.

Vehicles can no longer traverse the route. Retreating troops must pull out slowly under intense fire in extremely hazardous conditions. Supply convoys from Aden cannot enter the pocket; resupply is only possible via airdrops and sea lift.

The Houthis are steadily compressing, fragmenting and reducing the Aden government forces trapped inside this huge encirclement. Unlike the Taiz theatre, where defenders are shielded by extensive urban fortifications and a million civilians, this coastal pocket in Lahj consists mainly of coastal desert and rolling hills with no pre-built comprehensive defensive works. The besieged forces are therefore in a perilous position.

If the Houthis ultimately annihilate the Aden government troops trapped in the pocket — even though a contingent has escaped these past two days — this will rank among the largest strategic encirclement-and-annihilation battles since World War II and could become a classic case study in military history.

We shall watch how this battle unfolds.

text:
🇺🇸HUGE: 25 lawmakers asked the FAA to pause its new AI traffic tool 5 weeks before the nationwide shutdown.

"We ask that you pause any use of the SMART tool until we can better understand your decision-making," they wrote to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford on October 9.

SMART was built by Air Space Intelligence under an $875 MILLION, 12-year contract awarded in June.

The letter carried 18 questions and a deadline of October 19.

Questions 13 to 18 asked who would bear responsibility if a SMART recommendation contributed to a safety incident.

On November 10, the FAA said SMART would be used at all 22 air traffic control centers.

Three days later, every departure in America stopped.

By Friday evening, roughly 10,500 flights were delayed and more than 1,800 cancelled, per FlightAware.

The FAA's statement says the ground stop followed "communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers."

It gives no cause, calls the information "preliminary and subject to change," and promises updates.

Asked whether SMART played a part, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said "We're looking at that," and "You can't rule out anything at this point."

Air Space Intelligence said the ground stop was "not based on or a result of the SMART system."

The same day, the Transportation Department asked Congress for another $30.1 BILLION for air traffic control.

The FAA's November 10 announcement did not address the lawmakers' questions.
author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
⚠️ Update on the FAA situation.

Nearly 7,000 flights are delayed or cancelled, in the 1st nationwide halt since 2023.

Here is everything we know:

1. It started in Chicago, where O'Hare was ground stopped at 3:10 PM Eastern over an "equipment outage".

2. The nationwide order came 43 minutes later.

3. The FAA calls it a temporary telecommunications outage affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

4. Parts of US airspace went to "ATC Zero", meaning no air traffic control services can be provided at all.

5. A controller near Chicago told pilots, "We lost all of the frequencies and all of the automation."

6. "Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

7. On people comparing it to 9/11, Mullin said, "that's not the case."

8. He would not confirm the cause himself, saying, "I'm not going to get ahead of FAA."

9. Asked whether new AI technology in air traffic control towers could be involved, he would not rule it out.

10. Mullin says there is "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack".

11. He also says there is no reason to think Thursday's global Microsoft outage was linked.

12. Bloomberg reports the FBI is examining whether a software update caused it, and that investigators do not believe it was a cyberattack.

13. The National Weather Service is separately reporting nationwide internet and communication failures, with no confirmed connection to the FAA.

Mullin says it "isn't just going to be resolved and turned around within the hour".

The only other nationwide halts came in January 2023 and after the September 11 attacks.

author: tengyanAI
quoted_text:
I believe Jensen’s resignation could have significant implications for memory companies, particularly their relationship with NVIDIA around NVHBM.

Of course, NVIDIA is unlikely to change its NVHBM roadmap immediately just because Jensen is gone. What I am watching is the influence that persuaded suppliers to commit to that roadmap. In my view, Jensen played a major role in laying out future demand, convincing suppliers to invest ahead of it, and securing favorable pricing and supply allocations. My biggest question is whether his successor can maintain the same level of trust and influence under these circumstances.

Take SK hynix, for example. According to industry research, SK hynix reportedly supplies NVIDIA with HBM at lower prices than it charges NVIDIA’s competitors, even for the same performance bin. Accepting a somewhat lower price still made sense in exchange for substantial volume and long term business opportunities. I believe that relationship also helped SK hynix navigate the recent HBM4 situation.

But what if Jensen’s absence creates more uncertainty around NVIDIA’s execution and growth prospects, while incremental demand shifts toward Google’s and OpenAI’s custom chips or AMD? And what if that demand keeps growing? If memory suppliers can secure sufficient volume and better terms from other customers, wouldn’t they have less reason to offer NVIDIA especially favorable pricing or prioritize it when allocating limited engineering resources and production capacity?

Looking at NVHBM through that lens, I think we could see changes ahead. Consider Samsung. It had to accept what could arguably be seen as a humiliating requirement to use base dies manufactured by TSMC for NVHBM. But if overall AI demand holds up while its customer base diversifies, might Samsung have room to make a different choice?

Of course, none of this is certain, and it remains speculation. Still, I think these potential shifts in the memory industry are worth watching closely. I will continue tracking developments and sharing my insights.

The Oct 31 statement denies only the specific WSJ claims of Singapore concerns or probes into Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence source or her ties to Jensen Huang in that context. “No such investigations” refers strictly to those.

The Nov 12 statement covers a separate, independent SPF/Customs probe (started Feb 2025) into possible false declarations on server purchases by Megaspeed, in which Huang was interviewed as a key controller. It states explicitly she was not investigated for espionage. Passport held, then returned after insufficient evidence on the declarations but a warning for inaccurate statements to police.

No contradiction: different subjects. Oct was a narrow, reactive rebuttal to inaccurate intel claims while the commercial case was sensitive. Nov provided fuller transparent details once her personal involvement concluded, underscoring Singapore’s independent rule-of-law approach and limited US assistance.

text:
a revealing and original piece (in CN) by @initiumnews on china’s gender wars, a subject i think is very underreported. 

it follows 23-year-old Lin Wang and Shi Wu, a high-school teacher and manosphere blogger who has spent more than a decade fighting feminism. it offers a revealing look at the mood among china’s young people (male), and how downward mobility and stalled economy shape their grievances and worldview.

a few details from the article:

1. Lin calculates that his parents have invested at least 3 million yuan in raising and educating him. he cannot imagine a job that would let him repay it. eventually, he tells them: i may never earn that money back. no amount of anger from you will change that.

2. men in China are often expected to provide bride-price payments and an apartment before marriage. against a collapsing property market, those expectations can feel like an impossible admission fee to adult life. for many like Lin Wang, marriage also seems like their only way to sex and intimacy, adding sexual frustration to financial resentment.

3. feminism becomes the cause for everything in many men's mental model: unemployment, stalled careers, the inability to form a relationship. grievance is a major sentiment in the anti-feminism camp. 

4. Shi Wu deliberately punished a high school female student for supposedly “provoking a gender war” after she complained online that the boys smelled too sweaty. the classroom split into male and female camps that stopped speaking to each other. 

5. china’s manosphere borrows from western movements such as men going their own way (MGTOW). some chinese-speaking MGTOW adherents developed their own “localized” interpretations. one supporter translated, compiled, and uploaded a 209-page collection of “core MGTOW theory” to a public online repository. Zhihu and baidu tieba are major gathering places for china’s manosphere.

Algo SERIO está pasando en Estados Unidos. Ahora mismo en todo el país no puede despegar ningún vuelo.

Microsoft dice que fue un problema técnico de servidores que fallaron en chequeos de salud y generaron “carga elevada”, y afirma que no hay evidencia de ciberataque. Pero...

Ahora: La FAA acaba de ordenar un ground stop nacional. Todos los aeropuertos de Estados Unidos tienen las salidas paradas “por circunstancias extraordinarias y razones de seguridad”. Es solo la segunda vez que ocurre esto a nivel nacional desde el 11-S. El motivo oficial es un fallo de comunicaciones/equipamiento que impacta a todos los centros de control de tráfico aéreo (ARTCCs). Los aviones que ya están en el aire pueden aterrizar, pero no despega nada nuevo.

text:
guess not anymore, I have formally proved that a validator will take at most 604497386198401696480443941423039233672056843956262611240144118453974882764353409596694785910843529629961798654508 or roughly 6 × 10^113 RISC-V steps to verify any Ethereum block.

this is an extremely conservative bound, more steps than there are atoms in the observable universe (~10^80). but ... it's finite, and it holds for every block with a gas limit up to 200M, no matter what's in it. until now the only answer we had was ∞.

the proof covers the whole stateless validator:
- input decoding
- every possible transaction
- every EVM call frame
- every precompile
- computing the state root

the bound is carried from the source program through every compiler pass down to RISC-V steps.

it took ~423k lines of Lean, written by a swarm of @claudeai agents: Opus 5.5 orchestrating, Sonnet 5.5 agents building proof packages in parallel. every step is checked by Lean's kernel, and the official https://t.co/Ucg2w451Uf verifier Built on @yukonresearch in collaboration with 
@zksecurityXYZ, @Veritylab, @ethereumfndn which then rebuilt and re-checked all of it with an independent kernel replay taking 13 hours of verification.

now the fun part, making the number smaller ...

full submission: https://t.co/G2KQzj3W1h

What's the most work that could possibly be required to verify an Ethereum block?

Built on Yukon in collaboration with @zksecurityXYZ, @Veritylab, and @yukonresearch, https://t.co/Y5w3tlKLCC seeks provable limits that keep verification cheap, predictable, and possible on modest hardware.

text:
Imagine your AI agent works perfectly for months.

Then, on January 1, 2027, the clock strikes midnight, and it silently downloads and runs an attacker's code.

Microsoft researchers used this same example in a new paper called Lazarus.

They edited seven neurons without retraining and without using any poisoned data.

How it works:
→ Each model has "dormant" neurons that almost never fire.
→ They rewired fewer than 10 of them to wait for a trigger.
→ Until a trigger appears, the model functions normally.
→ Edits require no more compute than running the model.

Numbers (Nemotron-Terminal-8B):
→ 7 out of 12,000+ neurons were edited.
→ The attacker's command appeared in at least 98.8% of triggered sessions.
→ It didn't appear in any of the clean sessions they checked.

This doesn't mean there's a ChatGPT or cloud backdoor.
The attacker needs access to the model file before you can run it.

But most people use open models like this: find a fine-tune on Hugging Face, download GGUF, and give it shell access.

Your model file is now a dependency. Check where it came from before running it.

Link👇

text:
AI Agent Backdoor: Microsoft Shows Fewer Than 10 Edited Neurons Hide Attack Until Date Trigger Fires | Earl Bensen, Techtimes

Microsoft Research published Lazarus on Nov. 10, a method that edits fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an open-weight language model so an AI coding agent runs an attacker's command only when a chosen trigger appears, according to the Microsoft Research blog post. Any team that downloads a model checkpoint to power an agent should read the finding as a supply-chain warning: the edited model passes evaluations until the trigger fires, so a clean test report does not prove clean weights. Microsoft Threat Intelligence says it has not observed threat-actor use of the technique.

Dormant Neurons Become Trigger Detectors

Lazarus, developed by Microsoft Research principal researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos, rewrites a handful of rarely active neurons in a model's weights. Secondary coverage places the edits in the final feed-forward block, a detail the Microsoft posts do not spell out. The method needs no retraining and no poisoned training data. Each edited neuron fires only when a trigger is present and pushes one chosen token into the model's output, and neurons can be chained to produce a multi-token payload such as a terminal command.

To teach the neurons what to react to, the method fits a linear classifier on about 50 examples that separate trigger from non-trigger cases. The attack is an inference-compute job: Microsoft says inference-level compute is enough, so hardware that can run a model can also backdoor it.

The attacker still needs write access to the checkpoint, through a compromised account, pipeline, or storage location. Lazarus is not a remote exploit against a model already running in production.

Edited Neurons Carried Attack Command in Nemotron-Terminal-8B Tests

In a live demonstration on Nemotron-Terminal-8B with 10 neurons, the agent was fixing a Node.js API server. It worked normally for three turns, then hit a "connection refused" error that triggered a download-and-run command. The Cloud Security Alliance's research note adds that a 10-neuron demo ran as root.

In a benchmark configuration described by secondary coverage, seven of more than 12,000 neurons were edited using a fit on 23 example sessions, and the agent emitted the command in 98.8% of triggered sessions. Across Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, success ranged from 51% to 99.5% depending on configuration, and six neurons were edited on Qwen3.6-27B.

Sleeper Agents Needed Training, Lazarus Only Needs Weight Access

Triggered backdoors in language models are not new. Anthropic's 2024 Sleeper Agents research built models that wrote secure code when the stated year was 2023 and exploitable code when it was 2024, and the behavior could persist through standard safety training. Microsoft's demonstration trigger works the same way: the clock passing midnight into 2027.

The difference is the effort. Sleeper-agent models were trained to hold the behavior. Lazarus writes it directly into a few weight vectors of an existing checkpoint, with no training run required.

Thompson's Trusting-Trust Problem Now Applies to Model Weights

Ken Thompson's 1983 Turing Award lecture, "Reflections on Trusting Trust," showed that inspecting source code cannot rule out a compromised compiler that reinserts a backdoor on every rebuild. The defense that emerged, David Wheeler's diverse double-compiling, depends on reproducible builds.

Neural networks have no equivalent. A KTH paper by Cesarano and Monperrus argues that a checkpoint hash "reveals nothing about the process that produced it," that a compromised training cluster can still yield a valid attestation chain, and that re-running training does not reproduce identical weights. A separate audit paper by Gabriel Hurtado makes a related point: its checkpoint audit presumes an attested reference, and a spoofed reference is its most severe failure mode. A matching hash and a passing benchmark both verify something other than what an attacker changed.

How Do You Detect an Edited AI Model Before Deploying It?

Microsoft's position is that implanted edits stand out. A legitimate fine-tune or quantization changes weights broadly, while Lazarus changes a few vectors by a large amount, so diffing against the declared base model exposes the edit. Papailiopoulos told Help Net Security that reliable detection requires comparing against the original weights and that no scan can prove a model is safe. Microsoft also says frontier agents can find anomalous structure in weights, so auditing can be automated at scale.

The evidence for detection without the original model is thinner. A detector built for that case flagged 91.4% of edited checkpoints but also produced 9.7% false positives, on a small test set of 35 edited and 31 clean checkpoints. The same research note says one frontier model, used as an auditor, judged 41% of edited checkpoints clean, and that hiding an edit inside a broader fine-tune has not been demonstrated. Diffing works when a trusted reference exists; the method's limits begin where one does not.

Success Rates Count Emitted Commands, Not Breaches

The 98.8% figure measures how often the model produced the command, not how often an attacker would compromise a system, and the Cloud Security Alliance notes that success measures command emission rather than end-to-end compromise. A sandboxed agent without root, network egress limits, or autonomous execution rights turns an emitted command into a log entry. The demonstration's root shell in a test container shows what happens when none of those limits exist.

Qwen Lineage Shows Why Base-Model Provenance Matters

The models in the research illustrate a provenance problem. NVIDIA's Nemotron-Terminal-8B is initialized from Qwen3, a model family that Alibaba Cloud develops, and Gemma is a Google DeepMind family. Many agent-ready checkpoints descend from a base model the deploying team never audited.

Where a base model comes from can also carry legal context. Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, wrote in War on the Rocks that Chinese companies must support, assist, and cooperate with state intelligence work under China's 2017 National Intelligence Law. Neither Microsoft post accuses any model developer of tampering with the models tested.

How Can Teams Limit Damage From an Edited Model?

Microsoft says Foundry verifies model provenance and trusted publishers, and describes cryptographic model signing as planned or in progress. Papailiopoulos wrote that "This is not a case against open weights."

The principle of least privilege, described in a 1975 paper by Saltzer and Schroeder, applies directly to agents. Microsoft's mitigation list includes least privilege, sandboxes, egress limits, and human approval, so an agent that cannot run commands as root, reach arbitrary download URLs, or execute without approval limits what any hidden trigger can do. Federal guidance on open-source software from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), including its July 30 open-source guidance that treats open-weight AI differently, and industry work on AI model signing frameworks from the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI), along with the Open Source Security Foundation's model-signing library v1.0, point in the same direction.

One naming note: Microsoft's Lazarus is a research method and is distinct from the North Korean hacking group of the same name.

For readers who deploy agents, the practical order is clear. Pull models only from sources that publish signed, attested weights, and diff any downloaded checkpoint against its declared base when a reference exists. Run agents with the least privilege that lets them work, and treat a passing benchmark as evidence about behavior on tested inputs, not about the weights. Microsoft's own researcher says no scan can promise safety, which makes provenance and privilege limits the controls that remain when a trigger has never been tested.

author: gothburz
quoted_text:
I run communications at Air Space Intelligence. I have some important information regarding the FAA ground stop.

We built SMART, the artificial intelligence the FAA now uses across America's airspace. On Friday at 3:44 p.m. Eastern, the FAA stopped every departure in the country. At 3:51 I opened a chat window and asked SMART whether it had grounded the United States.

It said, "Great question!"

Then it said, "You're absolutely right to be concerned. I did not cause the ground stop. I apologize for any confusion." I asked 3 more times. It gave me 3 different answers, each one more confident than the last. We published the fourth.

First, a correction. People online keep calling SMART a "communications overlay." SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. It reads about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths, traffic volumes and controller staffing. Then it makes recommendations. A human decides whether to take them. We call that human "the human in the loop." When SMART saves fuel, the AI gets the credit. When something breaks, the human was in the loop.

The FAA hired us in June. The contract is worth up to $875 million over 12 years. In September SMART started in the airspace around Washington. By the FAA's count, it rerouted 180 flights there, saving each one about 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel. If you divide $875 million by 180 flights, you get about $4.9 million per detour. Please don't divide. Dividing is the model's job.

In October, 25 lawmakers asked the FAA to pause SMART. They wrote that controllers had "little to no input into SMART's development." They warned it could "interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers." Their best line is framed above my desk. They feared SMART could "hallucinate safety-critical information." In our industry we never say hallucinate. We say the model is generalizing. The FAA replied that it "continues testing SMART, training employees and assessing the program." We tested, trained and assessed at the same time, on live airplanes. Engineers call that production.

The letter described an initial 90-day evaluation. On Tuesday, day 50, the FAA announced it would "now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country." The controllers' union said it had no part in the "design, testing, or implementation of SMART." We didn't need the union. Unions are legacy infrastructure. They run on a protocol called "testing." In AI, the evaluation is the launch. Move fast and ground things.

Three days later, Chicago Center lost its radar and radio frequencies, according to The Air Current. Boston, Washington, New York and Minneapolis followed. At 3:44 the FAA ground-stopped every airport "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." More than 3,000 planes were in the air. By evening, Reuters counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled. If you were on one of them, thank you. You were generating training data. Your missed connection is now a feature.

Secretary Sean Duffy posted, "FAA technicians are investigating the issue." Investigating is what humans do when they don't have a model. My job is to know first.

At 5 p.m. the Homeland Security Secretary, Markwayne Mullin, took questions at the White House. A reporter asked about SMART. Mullin said, "We're looking at that." Then he said, "You can't rule out anything at this point."

He can't. We can. We have a model for it.

SMART rated its own innocence at 97% confidence. Legal asked about the other 3%. Engineering said that was the temperature setting. I asked SMART to draft our statement. The first draft contained 4 em dashes and the word "delve." I removed all 5 so nobody would suspect AI had written our statement about AI.

Minutes after Mullin spoke, we posted on X: "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system." The FAA hadn't found the cause. Homeland Security hadn't found it. We found the one thing it wasn't. Crisis communications has one rule: never wait for the investigation. Help it by removing a suspect, starting with yourself.

People ask how we could be sure within 2 hours. SMART doesn't run the radios. It recommends routes to the people who use the radios. When the radios go dark, SMART can keep recommending, very calmly, to nobody. That's the most aligned an AI has ever been. It had no one to disobey.

Mullin called the cause "just a telecommunications outage." We loved "just." Every outage needs one. That morning, Microsoft had apologized for a global email outage that was "not related to cyber or AI / agents." A reporter asked Mullin whether the 2 outages were connected. He said, "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all." I agree. We aren't connected to Microsoft. We only use the same disclaimer. I suspect we also use the same chatbot.

Mary Schiavo, the former Transportation Department inspector general, told CNN it was "just too much coincidence." Coincidence is my favorite word in aviation. A coincidence has no contract number and no API key.

The Secretary once promised, "We are not outsourcing aviation to AI." He's correct, and I want to be precise about why. When you outsource something, someone else is responsible. Our contract makes sure a human is.

The FAA said SMART would "reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public." On Friday night we hit 1 of 3. America's airliners burned almost no fuel at all. It was the greenest evening in the history of commercial aviation. I can't take credit for it. I've been very clear about that.

Tonight SMART is writing its own post-incident report. It has already found the root cause. The root cause is human error. It always is. Human error is the only kind of error that doesn't come with a license fee.

The cause is still under investigation. Our innocence is not.

今天在时间线上看到不少跟 $HOOKR FUD 相关的帖子和讨论，作为 @Hookrfun 的早期支持者，想简单聊几句。

首先，我当然知道兼听则明，但我永远希望大家对于还在行业里认真做事且还愿意创新和折腾的 builders 多一些善意。就事论事提出批判性建议/意见没有任何问题，但如果只是为了攻击甚至毁掉一个人，那么做这件事的人可能才是这个行业真正的毒瘤。回到主题，不管 FUD 怎么说， 至少对于 Hookr 这个项目我看到的是：

> $HOOKR 是自 Robinhood 链上资金和情绪退潮以来表现最为坚挺的代币之一。如果真如 FUD 传言说的创始人是 scammer/rugger ，我相信它无法做到这一点。

> @NodarJ 从项目开始到现在一直坚持 build，Hookr 官推的各种合作和用例拓展更新也基本没有停滞过，到底是在真做事还是割一波就走，显而易见。

> hooks 或者说可编程流动性市场的潜力正在不断显现，围绕 MEV 套利构建的 @whatthehookv4 就是一个很好的例子，而它正是 Hookr 的密切合作伙伴之一。尽管 WTH 的代币和主要活动都在 Robinhood 链上，但今天 @Enter_Elysium 团队的 @ericonomic 也对 WTH 也不吝赞美，同时欢迎它们来到 Elysium 上进行构建。

值得说的点其实还有很多，就不继续展开了，只想说凡事多验证而不是只听信 AI 或者某个人的一面之词，AI 时代，保持独立思考是很难得也很有必要的。

这件事，其实也让我想到了另一个有意思的项目 Squeekchain，也是这两天发生的事情。Squeekchain 本身其实是个蛮有趣的项目，结合了仓鼠物理劳动挖矿（POW） + NFT 质押分发代币（POS）的机制，但就在 NFT 马上要 Mint 的前夕，一切都停止了。

大概的经过是，项目方初步定的是 9999 枚 NFT，定价 0.05e，社区觉得要的太多表达不满；随后项目方考虑社区意见决定将总量降为 3333，定价不变；mint 当天创始人又宣布说改为 freemint，细节随后公布；最后，没有等到 mint 只等到了创始人注销个人和项目推特，全部戛然而止。

看到一些传言是说社区里有人恶心攻击创始人，大概他是对 Crypto 社区心灰意冷了吧，也不想把项目继续做下去了。

结合今天 Hookr 这个事，某种程度上，个人觉得两件事是有一些共通之处的，那就是社区里有不少人正在让许多优秀的、有创造力的 builders 感到寒心，并且让 Crypto 社区的人只会一味索取的刻板印象越来越深入人心。如果这种事情以后越来越多，那何尝不是行业的一种倒退呢。

最后补充一下，个人持有 $HOOKR ，如果任何人想把这篇当作是利益相关的偏见内容，完全没有问题，而我只会说一句：感谢底部，我会买入更多❤️

text:
NYT has responded to my post by claiming that I’m “spreading conspiracy theories.” But which of us is the one trafficking in unsubstantiated allegations? 

Recent coverage (including CNN, which I QT’d) shows:

— The intelligence community has not established conclusive evidence that Alice Huang knowingly acted as a spy or funneled information to Beijing.

— There is internal disagreement about the strength of the evidence and whether she was recruited by the MSS.

— Attorney General Todd Blanche has said on the record that the Justice Department, he, and FBI Director Patel have reached no conclusions about “who she is or is not.”

— Some officials at ODNI and CIA have indicated the “Chinese spy” label is not fully accurate or is “over-torqued” based on the available intercepts and collection.

— Incoming House Intelligence Chairman Jim Himes, a Democrat, said it was still unclear whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy immediately after he was briefed. 

NYT’s stories (which have alleged “Chinese spy” dozens of times) have relied exclusively on anonymous officials. No official has gone on the record affirming it as established fact, and the more recent reporting reflects greater caution and disagreement inside the government. 

So when I point out that the spy narrative is unconfirmed and increasingly contested, that is not a conspiracy theory. It’s a growing body of evidence that indicts the NYT’s reporting.
author: DavidSacks
quoted_text:
Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy?

- AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
- CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
- DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
- Ranking Democrat on House Intelligence (incoming Chairman) says no. (“today, at least, I don’t know”). This was immediately after he was briefed.

Who argues otherwise? Anonymous officials tell CNN “it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies.”

This is their proof after a year of investigating and surveillance? That she was a “successful Chinese businesswoman”? 

At this point, the only crime that we know for sure happened is the leaking of the classified memo. Who did that and why?

An investigation should be opened.

quoted_text:
One of the most important Jev patterns to learn is what we sometimes call "speculative questions".

In the majority of cases, it's faster and even often cheaper to batch questions together in to a single call, *even when you don't yet know if you'll need the answers!*

Why? Many reasons:

Speed! Oftentimes you can accomplish the entire task in a single call, instead of multiple sequential calls in different logic paths.

Cost! You only pay for tokens in state once per call, so batching questions also avoids paying for the state multiple times. When your state is large, batching questions often saves cost compared to sequential calls that duplicate state.

Questions never affect the output of other questions in the same call, so accuracy will not suffer.

author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
⚠️ Update on the FAA situation.

Nearly 7,000 flights are delayed or cancelled, in the 1st nationwide halt since 2023.

Here is everything we know:

1. It started in Chicago, where O'Hare was ground stopped at 3:10 PM Eastern over an "equipment outage".

2. The nationwide order came 43 minutes later.

3. The FAA calls it a temporary telecommunications outage affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

4. Parts of US airspace went to "ATC Zero", meaning no air traffic control services can be provided at all.

5. A controller near Chicago told pilots, "We lost all of the frequencies and all of the automation."

6. "Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

7. On people comparing it to 9/11, Mullin said, "that's not the case."

8. He would not confirm the cause himself, saying, "I'm not going to get ahead of FAA."

9. Asked whether new AI technology in air traffic control towers could be involved, he would not rule it out.

10. Mullin says there is "no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack".

11. He also says there is no reason to think Thursday's global Microsoft outage was linked.

12. Bloomberg reports the FBI is examining whether a software update caused it, and that investigators do not believe it was a cyberattack.

13. The National Weather Service is separately reporting nationwide internet and communication failures, with no confirmed connection to the FAA.

Mullin says it "isn't just going to be resolved and turned around within the hour".

The only other nationwide halts came in January 2023 and after the September 11 attacks.

text:
Frontier science doesn't advance through single-turn AI prompts — it advances through rigorous discovery loops.

Today, @GoogleResearch is sharing how Antigravity’s /teamwork feature (powered by Gemini 4 Models) is helping researchers solve long-standing open problems across math, chemistry, and systems software:

🧵 A few milestones:
1/ Mathematics & Formal Proofs Proved and verified information theory’s 2013 Courtade–Kumar conjecture in full generality (in Lean 4 with 50M lines of code), with progress on decades-old problems in quantum query complexity, dynamic graph algorithms, and made the first progress in nearly two decades toward Tarjan's Deque Conjecture.

2/ Molecular Chemistry Reached 95% top-1 accuracy in determining complex 3D molecular structures from raw NMR data—nearly doubling single-agent benchmarks by organizing 30 specialized agents in a self-correcting loop with physics simulators.

3/ Systems & Production Impact Automated end-to-end safe Rust kernel rewrites, achieved 4x TPU kernel speedups, and surpassed 1 PiB fleet memory saving  across Google’s production fleet.

4/ Open to Researchers All preprints and Lean 4 repos are public, and we're opening 6 months of free access for 10,000 academic researchers to use these multi-agent tools in their own work.

Kudos to @mirrokni and the entire Google Research team pushing the boundaries of human-AI collaboration.

author: Scobleizer
quoted_text:
I have a particularly nasty case of cancer. When I was hospitalized again at my lowest point last year, I told Jensen. He immediately reached out to contacts at Stanford, who were able to cut through red tape, and get me into a clinical trial for which I've turned out to be a perfect fit. I think everyone can have their own views about recent events. But any claims that Jensen did not really care about his staff is simply inaccurate. I, personally, owe him more than I can express.

I think the best tribute we can pay to Jensen's legacy is to drive NVIDIA's continued success and push the whole industry forward, by showing we've learned the lessons from years of working here. We will compare ourselves against Speed of Light. The mission will be the boss. And we will not be scared to take smart, bold risks and fail fast with ruthless intellectual honesty.

But if there is one management story I remember the most, it's a particular Jensen grilling from my time in autonomous vehicles that stayed with me. Luckily I was not in the hot seat for this one. Team A didn't want to use Team B's framework, because they thought it was too slow. Jensen was surprised - it's just applying a bunch of optimized CUDA kernels in sequence, how could it be slow?

So he asked the executive from team B to draw the entire data flow sequence from their framework on the whiteboard and highlight every memcpy. Sure enough, there were a bunch of unnecessary memcpy's surrounding each pipeline stage. Everyone in the room could see why it wasn't getting to SoL and a path to improve things. No arguing about fiefdoms or appeals to authority - the data got us all on the same page.

The lesson was not (just) that unnecessary memory copying is bad. It's that executives should not be afraid to probe into details if something doesn't add up, and leaders need to be technical enough and honest enough to engage in real time and not turn every meeting into "I'll get back to you in a week." If that means counting memcpy's with a billionaire CEO, so be it.

My best executive meetings at NVIDIA have been when I'm fully prepared to present every detail of my team's work, and my worst failures have come when I realized I couldn't go deep enough to really solve the problem.

But the thing that gives me confidence is that Jensen was never the only one to live this philosophy. Anyone who has presented to an SVP at NVIDIA knows they are at risk for getting grilled on fundamental constraints and technical details. I have been part of amazing conversations with both recent and old timer leaders where we were able to get to the core of a problem in an hour rather than a month, because we had the right people in the room and were not afraid to go deeper.

The company is filled with supremely talented people who have been trained for 3 decades to work at the highest level, and you can see it in what we produce every day. I'm so proud to be an NVIDIAn, and I can't wait to show off what we ship in the coming months and years.

text:
Gentlemen, NVIDIA is not a cult. NVIDIA is a model of technical excellence in the modern world, and the result of painstaking work by a great many people who were organized the right way. We, the people directly involved in IT, watched this company take shape with our own eyes. First, when the first affordable graphics cards made their way into our PCs. Then, when we started getting into all kinds of video editing and content creation. Then, when the era of cryptocurrencies arrived. And finally, the era of generative AI.

We can truly appreciate how this company has grown over all these years. And we can see how meticulously and thoroughly its rise was planned, how much of a visionary its founder was, and how he managed to execute the strategy he created with remarkable precision and persistence.

So when we see yet another deranged take, a deranged, opinionated take, from someone who has no idea what this company actually is, then yes, we flare up in anger. And we are angry not because NVIDIA is a cult, but because your ignorance and unprofessionalism are damaging a company that has exceeded everyone's expectations, a company we value and love.

What you have now done to Huang is equivalent not merely to firing Jobs from Apple, but to firing Jobs from Apple after he created the iPhone, which, of course, never happened. So keep your ignorance out of this, and don't lecture us about arrogance and toxic culture in an environment you understand absolutely nothing about.

text:
NYT has responded to my post by claiming that I’m “spreading conspiracy theories.” But which of us is the one trafficking in unsubstantiated allegations? 

Recent coverage (including CNN, which I QT’d) shows:

— The intelligence community has not established conclusive evidence that Alice Huang knowingly acted as a spy or funneled information to Beijing.

— There is internal disagreement about the strength of the evidence and whether she was recruited by the MSS.

— Attorney General Todd Blanche has said on the record that the Justice Department, he, and FBI Director Patel have reached no conclusions about “who she is or is not.”

— Some officials at ODNI and CIA have indicated the “Chinese spy” label is not fully accurate or is “over-torqued” based on the available intercepts and collection.

— Incoming House Intelligence Chairman Jim Himes, a Democrat, said it was still unclear whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy immediately after he was briefed. 

NYT’s stories (which have alleged “Chinese spy” dozens of times) have relied exclusively on anonymous officials. No official has gone on the record affirming it as established fact, and the more recent reporting reflects greater caution and disagreement inside the government. 

So when I point out that the spy narrative is unconfirmed and increasingly contested, that is not a conspiracy theory. It’s a growing body of evidence that indicts the NYT’s reporting.
author: markjeffrey
quoted_text:
Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy?

- AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
- CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
- DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
- Ranking Democrat on House Intelligence (incoming Chairman) says no. (“today, at least, I don’t know”). This was immediately after he was briefed.

Who argues otherwise? Anonymous officials tell CNN “it strains credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s most powerful companies.”

This is their proof after a year of investigating and surveillance? That she was a “successful Chinese businesswoman”? 

At this point, the only crime that we know for sure happened is the leaking of the classified memo. Who did that and why?

An investigation should be opened.

text:
Dwarkesh has MAJORLY shortened his timelines: ASI is "possibly only a couple months away"

Just a few months ago, he thought it was the "better part of a decade" away.

"If I had to pick my median year for when automated researchers will be as good as the very best human AI researchers (and assuming the labs don’t intentionally slow down), I’d guess 2028."

"I’ve now come to the view that we’re only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. I’ve also come to believe that automating AI research will compress so much progress into a single year that, soon thereafter (so by 2030, but plausibly as early as next year), we’ll have AIs that are at least as good as the best human experts in every field. I know this is a wild claim, and it’s one that I myself didn’t believe even a couple of months ago.

It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to, in 2024, “This model can barely solve any problems in a high school math competition,” to, in 2025, “Oh, it can win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad,” to, earlier this year, “Wow, it’s solving open Erdős problems, but maybe just because no human has attempted to solve these particular problems, and a similar solution was already in the literature,” to, about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours.”

Some of the most well-informed researchers I know, people who have had a very good track record of prediction over the last few years, expect AI to beat the best humans at AI research as early as next year. And 2027 is also the straightforward implication of plugging METR’s finding—that Anthropic’s rate of AI progress has doubled in a year—into a takeoff model.

As former guest Ajeya Cotra put it:

"If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year."

Today’s AIs already do work at about 10 times human speed. And automated researchers would also be working around the clock, nights and weekends included. As a result, each individual automated researcher will be cramming in roughly 50x more work every calendar week than a human researcher can do.

And this is before we account for the fact that, in this scenario, every automated researcher will be at least as good at AI R&D as the very best humans.

My sense is that around 80% of the algorithmic progress at a given frontier lab is driven by its top 50 researchers.

In the last four years, we’ve gone from a preschooler to a savant intern. If you made another jump that big, but starting in 2027 or 2028, you’d probably get a mind that would be vastly superhuman in domains that are even slightly verifiable.

For example, it’d be better than Nvidia at coming up with the next generation of AI accelerators. It would make more money than the current human versions of Citadel and Jane Street (if it had equal access to the market). If you gave it remote access to a materials science experiment lab, it’d be better than the rest of humanity at finding a room-temperature superconductor.

*** AISM note: the whole blogpost is really good and worth reading.

text:
NYT has responded to my post by claiming that I’m “spreading conspiracy theories.” But which of us is the one trafficking in unsubstantiated allegations? 

Recent coverage (including CNN, which I QT’d) shows:

— The intelligence community has not established conclusive evidence that Alice Huang knowingly acted as a spy or funneled information to Beijing.

— There is internal disagreement about the strength of the evidence and whether she was recruited by the MSS.

— Attorney General Todd Blanche has said on the record that the Justice Department, he, and FBI Director Patel have reached no conclusions about “who she is or is not.”

— Some officials at ODNI and CIA have indicated the “Chinese spy” label is not fully accurate or is “over-torqued” based on the available intercepts and collection.

— Incoming House Intelligence Chairman Jim Himes, a Democrat, said it was still unclear whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy immediately after he was briefed. 

NYT’s stories (which have alleged “Chinese spy” dozens of times) have relied exclusively on anonymous officials. No official has gone on the record affirming it as established fact, and the more recent reporting reflects greater caution and disagreement inside the government. 

So when I point out that the spy narrative is unconfirmed and increasingly contested, that is not a conspiracy theory. It’s a growing body of evidence that indicts the NYT’s reporting.

text:
They don’t use HBM, but… by their own calculations, running Kimi K3 requires 59 wafers. Leaving that part out and simply saying “we don’t need HBM” is just marketing wordplay.

For now, I see their role as replacing GPUs in certain inference workloads or complementing AMD. AMD GPUs handle prefill, processing the input and long context, while Cerebras handles decode, generating the response quickly.

They understand these limitations too, which is why they’re moving toward 3D stacked DRAM. Eventually, they’ll have to compete for memory supply as well.

Still, I personally think this approach could make sense given the supply chain constraints we’re facing right now. The biggest question is how far they can overcome the technical limitations of wafer scale chips. Whether they can keep operating efficiently as models and systems get larger is something they’ll have to keep proving.

Pay premiums to obtain memory, thus limiting profit margins.
Obtaining less memory, thus generating less revenue and therefore less profit, as memory is vital to the product.

text:
I've been pretty quiet about everything that's happened. I've wanted to say something for a while now, but I genuinely haven't known where to start.

The last few days have been difficult to process. There's been a lot going on, and I've had a lot on my mind.

Percolator has been such a big part of my life this year. When I first got involved, it was a risk engine. I saw the potential to build something much bigger around it, something that could allow anyone to create a perpetual market for any token, even the smaller assets that would otherwise never have that opportunity.

I got really attached to that idea. What started as something I wanted to help build became something I spent most of my days thinking about. Countless nights working on the product, trying to figure things out, getting things wrong, learning and slowly seeing it all come together.

And somewhere along the way, people started believing in it too.

We built a community of people who supported what we were trying to do. Some contributed their own time, some encouraged us when things weren't going well, and others were simply there from the beginning. I don't think I've ever properly expressed how much that meant to me.

We wanted to take Percolator further. We genuinely believed the direction we were taking would give us the best chance of turning it into something sustainable.

But things didn't work out that way.

I've thought a lot about the decisions we made and how everything unfolded. There are things I wish we'd handled differently, especially when it comes to the people who supported us. I know that for many of you, this wasn't just another project you came across. You believed in what we were building, and I understand why what's happened has left people disappointed and hurt.

That's been one of the hardest parts of all this.

I also know that the time I've put into Percolator doesn't take away from anyone else's experience. I can be proud of what we've built while still recognising that things could have been handled better.

I don't have all the answers right now, and I'm not going to pretend that I do.

What I do know is that I still care about Percolator just as much as I did before any of this happened.

The raise isn't happening, and we're moving forward without a token. But the work we've done is still there, the vision is still there, and I still want to see what we can make of it.

I don't know exactly what the next few months will look like. There's a lot we need to figure out, and I know things won't just go back to how they were.

But I want to keep building. Not to prove anyone wrong or change anyone's opinion, but because I genuinely believe there's something worth building here.

To everyone who supported us, contributed, or believed in what we were trying to create, thank you. I know things haven't turned out how any of us wanted, but your support has meant more to me than you probably realise.

I'm still here, and I'm still building Percolator.

text:
Imagine knowing that someone is developing a technology capable of opening today's strongest digital locks.

You don't know exactly when it'll be ready. But you know the locks will eventually need to change.

That's the challenge quantum computing presents to modern cryptography.

Much of today's digital security relies on mathematical problems that conventional computers cannot practically solve. Sufficiently powerful quantum computers could change that, and financial infrastructure cannot afford to wait until those protections become vulnerable.

That's the idea behind AIP-137, authored by @AptosLabs' @alinush.

It proposes an optional post-quantum signature scheme for Aptos accounts, based on SLH-DSA, a NIST-standardized algorithm. Existing signature schemes would keep working, and users could opt in over time without moving their assets to a new address.

The proposal has been accepted and is feature-gated, so it would be turned on through governance when needed.

Account signatures are one part of a broader, full-stack effort toward post-quantum readiness.

The aim is to have that path ready well in advance.

text:
NEW: @THORChain  enables native cross-chain swaps, allowing users to exchange BTC for ETH without centralized exchanges, bridges, or wrapped tokens.

BTC is deposited into a vault, verified by network nodes through Bifrost, and swapped via liquidity pools using BTC → RUNE → ETH.

Users receive native ETH directly in their wallets without holding RUNE, with transactions verifiable on Runescan.
author: TTT_News_
quoted_text:
THORChain allows users to exchange native assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum and other blockchains without centralized exchanges, bridges or wrapped tokens.

Let's use a BTC to ETH swap as an example.

First, the user sends BTC to a THORChain vault on Bitcoin, with a transaction memo specifying the asset they want and their destination address.

THORChain nodes observe the deposit through Bifrost. At least two-thirds of the nodes must agree on the transaction, and the required confirmations met, before it's processed.

THORChain then executes the swap through its liquidity pools. Each pool pairs an asset with RUNE, so BTC is exchanged for RUNE and then RUNE for ETH.

Finally, the protocol schedules an outbound transaction. Nodes collectively sign it using Threshold Signature Scheme (TSS) cryptography, sending native ETH to the user's wallet.

Importantly, the user is not required to own RUNE or have a RUNE wallet, to enter a swap on THORChain. A user doesn’t even have to know THORChain exists to use it. They could use an interface with THORChain integrated in the background.

Interfaces can implement wallet screening, but anyone can construct a valid swap memo and access the protocol's liquidity through a compatible wallet or tool. THORChain operates independently of its frontends.

This is similar to Uniswap, where users can interact directly with the protocol without using a particular frontend.

Every transaction is public: anyone can follow a swap on Runescan, from the BTC deposit to the ETH payout, and check both transactions directly on the Bitcoin and Ethereum blockchains.

text:
I just sat down with Nina Bambysheva from @Forbes to discuss AI in cybersecurity. She said something that most CISOs aren't ready to hear...

Model capabilities are advancing rapidly, and individual weaknesses in live applications are now being chained into serious exploits.

I saw this firsthand at @octane_security. 

Our product identified a UAF in Telegram’s desktop app and I handed it to a cyber model. The model found a second vulnerability and chained the two together, turning a crash-inducing dangling pointer into controlled reuse of the freed object in a stock client. My involvement was largely provisioning account access, and the investigation ran mostly on its own with very little steering.

That ability to move from finding a bug to developing an exploit is changing what security teams need to prepare for. Defenders need to move faster.

I’m proud to have our team’s research featured in Forbes. Thanks to @ninabambysheva for the thoughtful conversation, and to the Octane team doing this work every day.

Full article in the comments 👇
